name: Industrial Policy
description: Iranian industrial policy concerns the development of productive firms, industrial employment, and manufacturing capabilities. Historical policy assessments and international cooperation documents show recurring tensions between domestic production, access to technology, private enterprise, and environmental performance. [s1][s2]

seo.title: Industrial Policy in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore the historical foundations of Iranian industrial policy, support for productive firms, and the relationship between manufacturing and environmental performance.

content.heading: Reconstruction and the industrial policy inheritance
content.content:
Iran's industrial policy cannot be understood solely as a list of factories or production targets. A World Bank assessment published in 1993 described an industrial economy shaped by the revolution of 1979, the subsequent war with Iraq, disrupted trade and finance, capital flight, and a dominant public sector. Its diagnosis linked industrial difficulties to price controls, foreign-exchange allocation, regulation, and weaknesses in markets and enterprise incentives. These were the Bank's findings about a particular historical period, rather than a description verified for present-day Iran. [s1]

The report described the first postwar development plan, covering 1989–1993, as seeking greater industrial output, improved use of existing capacity, more industrial exports, reduced dependence on imported capital goods, and a larger private-sector role. These were objectives, not demonstrated achievements. The distinction matters: announcing capacity or export targets does not establish that enterprises became more productive, competitive, or financially sustainable. [s1]

content.heading: Building capabilities within firms
content.content:
The United Nations Industrial Development Organization, or UNIDO, describes its work in Iran as supporting inclusive and sustainable industrial development. Its country factsheet identifies small and medium enterprise development, resource-efficient and low-carbon production, and environment and climate change as strategic areas. This gives a more concrete meaning to industrial development than simply increasing physical output: it includes how firms use energy and materials and whether productive activity creates employment. [s2]

The assistance described includes technology transfer, value-chain development, marketing, and trade capacity. A value chain connects the activities needed to turn inputs into products and bring them to customers. Work on these connections can address capabilities outside the factory itself, including suppliers and access to markets. UNIDO states that it works with private firms and government bodies, across enterprises of different sizes. Its factsheet establishes the scope of that cooperation; it does not independently demonstrate economy-wide productivity gains. [s2]

content.heading: What would demonstrate industrial progress?
content.content:
A useful assessment separates policy instruments from results. The historical World Bank study examined investment licensing, taxation, industrial finance, foreign investment, and infrastructure as distinct parts of the business environment. UNIDO's cooperation framework adds resource efficiency and enterprise capabilities. Together, these sources suggest questions for evaluation: can firms invest, obtain useful technology, reach customers, and reduce the resources needed for production? This is an editorial framework drawn from their subject coverage, rather than a verified account of current policy effectiveness. [s1][s2]

The World Bank maintains a manufacturing value-added indicator for Iran, expressed as a share of gross domestic product. Such a measure can describe manufacturing's relative economic weight, but it cannot by itself establish why that share changed or whether a particular intervention succeeded. The inspected page did not expose annual observations in retrievable text, so this page presents no numerical trend. [s3]

name: Education Policy
description: Education policy in Iran combines constitutional commitments with decisions about school access, learning support, and administration. Evidence on disability inclusion and refugee education shows why formal eligibility, practical admission, and meaningful participation require separate assessment. [s1][s2][s4]

seo.title: Education Policy in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand Iran's education commitments, school administration, disability inclusion, refugee access, and efforts to address learning gaps.

content.heading: From educational rights to school administration
content.content:
Iran's constitutional framework includes a commitment to free education through secondary school. UNESCO's education-policy profile also describes a commitment to expanding free higher education within the country's capacity. These are formal obligations; they do not establish that every child can reach a suitable school or receive the support needed to learn. [s1]

For primary and secondary inclusion, the profile identifies the Ministry of Education, provincial organizations, and district offices as administrative actors. It describes the Supreme Council of Education as approving education policies and regulations. This distinction helps international readers separate national policy decisions from the local arrangements through which children encounter the system. The profile is a documentary account and does not verify administrative practice in every province. [s1]

content.heading: Inclusion requires more than admission
content.content:
Inclusive education means enabling children with disabilities to participate in ordinary learning environments with appropriate support. Human Rights Watch's 2019 investigation identified barriers involving assessment procedures, inaccessible buildings, discriminatory attitudes, and insufficient preparation of school staff. It also acknowledged measures such as accessible materials and requirements for new or renovated buildings. Its criticism concerned the gap between those measures and equal access in practice. These findings describe the investigation's period and should not be treated as a fresh survey of every school. [s2]

A subsequent UNICEF announcement described SIRAT, translated as the Integrated System for Development and Education. The initiative sought to strengthen early identification, intervention, and referral within mainstream education. Teacher training and access to specialized support were central to the announced approach. The release documents an intervention and its intended expansion; it does not provide a completed national evaluation of learning or participation outcomes. [s3]

content.title: The support pathway described for SIRAT
content.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A["Teacher training"] -->|"Builds capacity for"| B["Early identification of support needs"]
  B -->|"Informs"| C["Timely intervention"]

```
content.summary: This diagram summarizes UNICEF's announced support approach. The arrows describe the intended educational process, not measured completion rates or a guarantee of service availability.

content.heading: Refugee access and the limits of capacity
content.content:
Refugee education illustrates why broad commitments need to be checked against dated admission arrangements. UNHCR's January–September 2024 factsheet described foreign children studying alongside Iranian children, while also reporting constraints from school capacity, household economic conditions, and documentation. It stated that foreign pupils required a Yekta identification code to register and that admission depended on available places. These are reported arrangements for that period, not current enrollment instructions. [s4]

The practical policy problem therefore extends beyond permission to enroll. A place in a classroom, affordable participation, and continuity of attendance all matter. UNHCR reported that economic difficulties and insufficient capacity were hampering access and contributing to dropout among Afghan children. Its account supports distinguishing inclusion as a policy commitment from inclusion as an experience. [s4]

content.heading: Addressing learning gaps
content.content:
A UNICEF report from September 2024 described remedial education in Khorasan Razavi and Fars for Afghan and host-community children who had struggled academically. The programme combined reading, writing, mathematics, and social and emotional learning with sessions helping parents support their children. It provides a concrete example of geographically targeted assistance rather than evidence of uniform national provision. [s5]

Taken together, these sources show why education policy should be assessed through both access and learning. An enrollment count cannot reveal whether buildings are accessible, referrals produce support, or children recover missed learning. Those questions require outcome evidence alongside administrative and programme descriptions. [s2][s3][s5]

name: Environmental Policy
description: Environmental policy in Iran links a constitutional commitment to environmental protection with practical questions about water use, pollution, land degradation, and ecosystem conservation. Groundwater research and wetland programmes illustrate the importance of distinguishing legal commitments, management interventions, and measured environmental outcomes. [s1][s2][s3]

seo.title: Environmental Policy in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore Iran's environmental commitments, groundwater constraints, wetland conservation programmes, and the evidence needed to assess policy outcomes.

content.heading: Environmental protection as a public responsibility
content.content:
Article 50 of Iran's constitution frames environmental protection as a public duty and prohibits economic activity associated with pollution or irreparable environmental destruction. A World Bank environmental assessment published in 2005 reproduced that commitment while identifying deterioration in water, air, land, and forest resources. Its central distinction remains useful for reading policy documents: a legal obligation and an environmental outcome are different kinds of evidence. The report's diagnosis is historical, not a measurement of conditions at the current cutoff. [s1]

The assessment organized environmental costs across water, air, land resources, forests, and coastal areas. This broad scope helps explain why environmental policy extends beyond protected landscapes. Urban pollution, agricultural land management, wastewater, and coastal ecosystems can all fall within its concerns. The report's old cost estimates are not presented here as current losses, and no monetary values have been updated without supporting data. [s1]

content.heading: Why falling extraction can signal worsening scarcity
content.content:
A peer-reviewed study by Noori and colleagues examined national groundwater records for 2002–2015. It found declining groundwater quantity and deteriorating quality across much of Iran. Crucially, lower annual extraction did not necessarily demonstrate successful conservation: the authors identified depletion and salinization as major constraints on obtaining fresh groundwater. [s2]

The study also distinguished withdrawal from consumption and examined regional variation. This matters when interpreting irrigation improvements: reducing water applied at a field does not automatically establish an equivalent improvement in basin water balance. Return flows and recharge must also be considered. The endpoint comparison below is historical and cannot establish the trajectory after 2015. [s2]

content.title: Reported national groundwater withdrawal: historical endpoints

content.heading: Wetlands connect conservation with livelihoods
content.content:
Wetland restoration provides a concrete example of policy crossing institutional and geographic boundaries. UNDP's May 2025 factsheet describes the Conservation of Iranian Wetlands Project as combining basin management, sustainable agriculture, biodiversity conservation, and alternative livelihoods. It identifies the Department of Environment and Ministry of Agriculture Jihad among its implementing partners, alongside Japanese support. [s3]

The factsheet lists work at Lake Urmia, Shadegan, Bakhtegan, Parishan, and Anzali. These are distinct project locations; their inclusion does not imply identical environmental conditions or recovery. It also identifies weak enforcement, pollution, and insufficient coordination between organizations as obstacles. This institutional account is useful evidence about programme design and recognized challenges, but its reported achievements need independent evaluation. [s3]

In December 2024, UNDP announced further Japanese support for wetland management and climate resilience. The announcement described planned cooperation with the Department of Environment and the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, or FAO, extending to 2028. Its emphasis on water-efficient agriculture and alternative livelihoods shows the intended connection between conservation and local economic activity. An announced implementation period does not demonstrate that restoration has been completed. [s4]

content.heading: Assessing results at the right scale
content.content: These examples point to a practical standard for evaluating environmental policy: compare interventions with conditions in the relevant ecosystem. A project may document training or changed farming practices while the wider basin remains under pressure. Conversely, a national average can conceal different local conditions. Groundwater research and wetland programme documents therefore need to be read together, with their different methods and reporting periods made explicit. Neither a project announcement nor a historical national trend alone establishes present environmental recovery. [s2][s3][s4]

datasets.population_scope: Groundwater extraction from deep wells, semideep wells, qanats, and springs covered by the study's national water-resources records
datasets.methodology: Selected endpoint values explicitly reported by Noori and colleagues from the Iran Water Resources Management Company dataset. National aggregates combine measurements and source estimates, including estimates for unmeasured extraction points. Values describe annual withdrawal, not net depletion, consumption, or stored groundwater. Only the two explicitly transcribed endpoints are included; this is not a complete annual series. Source period boundaries were not established, so Gregorian start and end dates are null.
